n: Murphy Report — Archdiocese of Dublin
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin
d: The Commission of Investigation into the Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin reported on 26 November 2009. It examined a sample of 46 priests out of 102 within its remit; 320 people complained of abuse between 1975 and 2004. It found Archbishops McQuaid, Ryan, McNamara and Connell handled complaints badly and that the archdiocese had insured itself against abuse litigation from 1987. It also criticised the Gardaí, and the Garda Commissioner apologised.
cover: Abuse 'covered up' 1975–2004; bishops generally did not report to Gardaí before 1996; archdiocese took out insurance against abuse litigation from 1987; Gardaí knew of complaints against Fr Tony Walsh in 1990–91 and took no action
cite: Commission of Investigation, Report into the Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin (Murphy Report), 26 November 2009

n: Winter Commission — Archdiocese of St. John's
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of St. John's; Archbishop Alphonsus Penney
d: Archbishop Alphonsus Penney commissioned former Lieutenant Governor Gordon Winter in May 1989 to inquire into sexual abuse of children by clergy of the archdiocese. The 1990 report assigned Penney part of the blame for covering up abuse, and he resigned after its release.
cover: Report assigned Archbishop Penney part of the blame for covering up abuse
cite: Report of the Archdiocesan Commission of Enquiry into the Sexual Abuse of Children by Members of the Clergy (Winter Report), 1990

n: Munich and Freising abuse report (Westpfahl Spilker Wastl)
who: Archdiocese of Munich and Freising; former archbishops incl. Joseph Ratzinger, Friedrich Wetter, Reinhard Marx
d: The report commissioned by the archdiocese from law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, published 20 January 2022, covered 1945–2019 and found at least 497 victims and 261 possible perpetrators and accomplices, 173 of them priests. It found misconduct by Joseph Ratzinger (Archbishop 1977–1982, later Pope Benedict XVI) in four cases, Cardinal Wetter in 21 and Cardinal Marx in three. Ratzinger corrected his statement that he had not attended a 15 January 1980 meeting about priest Peter Hullermann, who was admitted to Munich in 1980 and later reoffended.
cover: Report found misconduct by archdiocesan leaders, including Joseph Ratzinger in four cases; only 4 of 173 accused priests were dismissed from the clerical state
cite: Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, 'Sexueller Missbrauch Minderjähriger und erwachsener Schutzbefohlener durch Kleriker sowie hauptamtliche Bedienstete im Bereich der Erzdiözese München und Freising von 1945 bis 2019', 20 January 2022

n: Peter Hullermann — transferred from Essen to Munich 1980
who: Archdiocese of Munich and Freising; Diocese of Essen
d: In January 1980 the Munich archdiocese under Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger approved receiving Fr Peter Hullermann for therapy after accusations of abusing minors. He was then given pastoral work, abused minors again, and in June 1986 was convicted, fined DM4,000 and given an 18-month suspended sentence. He stayed a priest until suspended on 14 March 2010. Then vicar general Gerhard Gruber took responsibility for readmitting him.
cover: Accused priest accepted into Munich for therapy in January 1980 with Cardinal Ratzinger's approval, then reassigned to pastoral work where he abused again; remained a priest until 2010
cite: Süddeutsche Zeitung reporting (2010) as cited in Wikipedia; Munich report 2022

n: Regensburger Domspatzen choir — Weber report
who: Regensburger Domspatzen cathedral choir and boarding schools, Diocese of Regensburg
d: Lawyer Ulrich Weber's final report of 18 July 2017 found 547 boys suffered physical and/or sexual violence at the cathedral choir's schools, 67 of them sexual violence, by 49 perpetrators (9 sexual). The worst violence was at the preparatory school in Etterzhausen and Pielenhofen. The report faulted Georg Ratzinger, choir director 1964–1994, for failing to intervene; he denied knowing of sexual abuse.
cover: Report faulted choir director Georg Ratzinger for 'looking away' and said former bishop Gerhard Ludwig Müller bore 'clear responsibility' for weaknesses in investigating
cite: Ulrich Weber, Abschlussbericht zu Gewalt und Missbrauch bei den Regensburger Domspatzen, 18 July 2017

n: Canisius-Kolleg Berlin and Jesuit schools
who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits), Canisius-Kolleg Berlin and St. Blasien
d: Former pupils told the headmaster of the Jesuit Canisius-Kolleg in 2004–2005 that two former teachers had abused them; after further reports in 2009–2010 the headmaster wrote to all former pupils in January 2010 and many more came forward, opening the German church scandal. The teachers could not be prosecuted because of time limits. A Jesuit, Fr Wolfgang S., admitted abusing pupils at St. Blasien in 1982–1984; the Jesuits said superiors helped him emigrate to South America.
cover: Superiors helped one admitted abuser, Fr Wolfgang S., emigrate to South America; offences time-barred
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Germany, citing Der Spiegel and Jesuit statements (2010)

n: Cardinal Groër affair and Klasnic victims' commission, Austria
who: Archdiocese of Vienna; Austrian Bishops' Conference; Independent Victims' Protection Commission (Klasnic Commission)
d: Archbishop of Vienna Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër stepped down in September 1995 after a former pupil, followed by others and some monks, accused him of sexual abuse; church authorities confirmed the allegations in February 1998 and he withdrew from public life. In spring 2010 the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission chaired by Waltraud Klasnic. By 31 August 2021 it had approved payments in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total. At Kremsmünster Abbey school, former director Alfons Mandorfer was jailed for 12 years in 2013 for abusing 24 pupils.
cite: Unabhängige Opferschutzkommission / Stiftung Opferschutz figures, as summarised in German Wikipedia

n: CIASE (Sauvé Commission) — Catholic Church in France
who: Catholic Church in France (commissioned by bishops and religious orders)
d: The Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church, chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé, reported on 5 October 2021. Using a population survey, it estimated about 216,000 people were abused as minors by clergy and religious since 1950, and over 330,000 including lay workers in church institutions. It estimated 2,900–3,200 abusers, about 3% of clergy, and called the phenomenon systemic.
cover: Commission called the abuse 'massive' and 'systemic' and said the church must accept institutional responsibility
cite: Commission indépendante sur les abus sexuels dans l'Église (CIASE), final report, 5 October 2021

n: Bernard Preynat and Cardinal Barbarin, Lyon
who: Archdiocese of Lyon; Fr Bernard Preynat; Cardinal Philippe Barbarin
d: Fr Bernard Preynat was accused of abusing about 80 Boy Scouts between 1971 and 1991. He was laicised by the Holy See on 5 July 2019 and on 16 March 2020 a Lyon court sentenced him to five years in prison. Cardinal Philippe Barbarin was convicted on 7 March 2019 of not reporting the abuse and given a six-month suspended sentence; the conviction was overturned on appeal and the Cour de cassation cleared him in April 2021. Pope Francis accepted his resignation on 6 March 2020.
cover: Cardinal Barbarin convicted in March 2019 of failing to report abuse (suspended six months), cleared on appeal and by France's highest court in April 2021
cite: Lyon Tribunal correctionnel, 16 March 2020; Wikipedia, Bernard Preynat

n: Spanish Ombudsman report on Church abuse
who: Catholic Church in Spain
d: Spain's first official inquiry into clergy abuse, an 800-page report by Ombudsman Ángel Gabilondo released in October 2023, included a population survey indicating 200,000 to 440,000 potential victims since 1940. Separately, Spain's Supreme Court in April 2019 upheld a 17-year-seven-month sentence for Fr José Fernández for abusing two 12-year-old boys, and complaints against Marist school teachers in Barcelona rose to 43 against 12 teachers by February 2019.
cite: Defensor del Pueblo, 'Informe sobre los abusos sexuales en el ámbito de la Iglesia católica', October 2023, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: University of Zurich pilot study — Catholic Church in Switzerland
who: Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders (commissioned study)
d: Historians at the University of Zurich, commissioned by the Swiss Bishops' Conference, published a pilot study in September 2023 on abuse in the Swiss Catholic Church since 1950. Its detailed figures could not be verified from a source opened for this dataset; see notes.
cite: University of Zurich, Pilotprojekt zur Geschichte sexuellen Missbrauchs im Umfeld der römisch-katholischen Kirche in der Schweiz seit Mitte des 20. Jahrhunderts, September 2023 (figures unverified here)

n: Independent Commission — Catholic Church in Portugal
who: Catholic Church in Portugal (commission set up by the bishops)
d: An independent commission set up by the Portuguese bishops reported in February 2023 that at least 4,815 children had been abused by clergy and others in the church since 1950.
cite: Comissão Independente para o Estudo dos Abusos Sexuais de Crianças na Igreja Católica Portuguesa, report of 13 February 2023, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Poland — bishops' 2019 figures, Sekielski films and sanctions on bishops
who: Polish Episcopal Conference; Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź; Bishop Edward Janiak; Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz
d: On 14 April 2019 the Polish Episcopal Conference reported about 382 priests accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. The Sekielski brothers' documentaries 'Tell No One' (2019, 8.1 million YouTube views in days) and 'Hide and Seek' (2020) led the Vatican to investigate bishops. Pope Francis ordered Bishop Edward Janiak to resign in June 2020 for protecting abusive priests, removed Archbishop Głódź in August 2020, and in November 2020 sanctioned Cardinal Gulbinowicz. In May 2019 Poland raised the maximum sentence for child sexual abuse to 30 years.
cover: Bishops sanctioned by the Vatican for protecting abusers: Janiak (Kalisz) ordered to resign June 2020; Głódź (Gdańsk) removed August 2020 after covering up abuse by Henryk Jankowski and Franciszek Cybula
cite: Polish Episcopal Conference statistics, 14 April 2019; Holy See nunciature statements 2020, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Antonio Provolo Institute for the Deaf, Verona
who: Compagnia di Maria per l'educazione dei sordomuti (Provolo Institute); Diocese of Verona
d: In 2010 three former students of the Verona school for deaf children went public and 65 former students signed statements that they or others had been abused by 24 priests and religious from the 1950s to the 1980s. Fr Nicola Corradi was first accused in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese in 2011, but continued working at the Provolo school in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016 and later convicted.
cover: Fr Nicola Corradi, accused in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese in 2011, was working at the institute's branch in Argentina, where he went on to abuse children
cite: Wikipedia, Antonio Provolo Institute for the Deaf; Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe

n: Próvolo Institute, Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza) — convictions 2019
who: Provolo Institute for the Deaf (Argentina branch); Fr Nicola Corradi, Fr Horacio Corbacho, gardener Armando Gómez; Sr Kumiko Kosaka charged
d: Priests Nicola Corradi (Italian) and Horacio Corbacho and other staff of the Provolo school for deaf children in Mendoza were arrested in 2016. On 25 November 2019 a Mendoza court convicted Corradi and Corbacho of sexually abusing 22 children, sentencing them to 42 and 45 years; gardener Armando Gómez received 18 years. Nun Kumiko Kosaka was charged in 2017 with abuse and cover-up.
cover: Corradi had been accused in Verona in 2009 yet continued at the Argentine school; Japanese nun Kumiko Kosaka charged with abuse and covering up
cite: Mendoza criminal court verdict, 25 November 2019, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Fr Julio César Grassi — Happy Children Foundation
who: Fr Julio César Grassi, Fundación Felices los Niños
d: Fr Julio César Grassi, who ran a foundation for poor children, was convicted by Oral Criminal Court 1 of Morón of one count of sexual abuse and one of corrupting a minor and sentenced to 15 years. He maintained his innocence and appealed.
cite: Morón Oral Criminal Court 1 verdict (2009), as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Fr Alfonso Pedrajas diary — Jesuits in Bolivia
who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits) in Bolivia
d: Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas (1943–2009) worked at Jesuit schools in Bolivia including the Juan XXIII boarding school in Cochabamba, which he later directed. His diary, published by El País on 30 April 2023, records that he abused more than 80 minors in the 1970s and 1980s. He confessed to a Jesuit superior in 1978; El País reported that seven provincial superiors and about ten clerics covered for him. He died in 2009 and was never prosecuted.
cover: Confessed to his instructor in 1978, who covered it up; El País reported seven provincial superiors and about ten Bolivian and Spanish clerics covered for him
cite: El País, 'Diario de un cura pederasta', 30 April 2023, as summarised by Spanish Wikipedia

n: Fernando Karadima, Bishop Barros and Chile's bishops' resignation offer
who: Archdiocese of Santiago; Fr Fernando Karadima; Bishop Juan Barros; Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati
d: Parishioners first reported Fr Fernando Karadima to Archbishop Fresno in 1984. The Vatican found him guilty of abusing minors on 16 January 2011 and Pope Francis laicised him on 28 September 2018. After defending Bishop Juan Barros in January 2018, Francis sent Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Jordi Bertomeu to investigate; in an 8 April 2018 letter he admitted 'serious mistakes' of judgement. All 34 bishops at a May 2018 meeting in Rome offered their resignations; seven, including Barros, had been accepted by September 2018. Courts ordered the archdiocese to pay damages to survivors in 2018–2019.
cover: Parishioners reported Karadima to Archbishop Fresno in 1984; Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a credible 2004–05 investigation; Barros, a Karadima protégé, made bishop of Osorno in 2015
cite: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith verdict 2011; Pope Francis letter to the bishops of Chile, 8 April 2018; Wikipedia

n: Marist Brothers Chile — Brother Abel Pérez
who: Marist Brothers in Chile
d: In 2017 the Chilean Marist Brothers acknowledged that Brother Abel Pérez abused at least 14 minors between the 1970s and 2000. He had confessed to superiors in 2010 and was then transferred to Peru. Police investigated complaints at many of the order's schools.
cover: After confessing to superiors in 2010, Pérez was transferred to Peru
cite: Marist Brothers Chile statement 2017, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana — suppressed by the Vatican 2025
who: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae; founder Luis Fernando Figari
d: Journalists Pedro Salinas and Paola Ugaz exposed abuse by founder Luis Fernando Figari and associates in the 2015 book 'Mitad monjes, mitad soldados'. Investigators commissioned by the group in 2016 concluded Figari and former members sexually abused minors and adults; in February 2017 the group gave Peruvian prosecutors information on abuse of minors by Figari and four former members, and the Vatican barred Figari from contact with members. After a 2023 mission by Archbishop Scicluna and Mgr Bertomeu, Figari was expelled in August 2024 and over a dozen others, including a bishop, in September–October 2024. Pope Francis signed a decree suppressing the Sodalitium on 14 January 2025.
cover: Abuse reported by journalists in 2015 after years of internal silence; journalists faced legal action; Vatican commission in 2023 led to mass expulsions
cite: Sodalitium-commissioned investigators' reports 2016–17; Holy See decrees 2024–25, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
d: Former seminarians said Maciel abused them in Spain and Rome in the 1940s–50s; a victim and a bishop wrote to the Vatican in 1976 and 1978, and formal charges were filed in 1998, but no trial followed. In May 2006 the Vatican ordered Maciel to a life of prayer and penance, and on 1 May 2010 it called his conduct 'true crimes' and said the Legion had shielded him. The Legion's own report of 21 December 2019 acknowledged 175 minors abused from 1941 to 2019: 60 by Maciel and the rest by 33 priests, 14 of whom had themselves been abused within the order.
cover: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried
cite: Legion of Christ, report on abuse 1941–2019, 21 December 2019; Holy See communiqué 1 May 2010, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Mexican bishops' conference — 426 priests investigated
who: Conferencia del Episcopado Mexicano
d: In January 2020 the Mexican Episcopal Conference said it had investigated 426 priests over the previous ten years for sexual abuse of minors and other crimes, and that 217 had been removed. El Universal reported on 2 February 2020 that only six of 156 alleged abuse cases involving minors from 2009 to 2019 ended in conviction.
cover: El Universal reported only six convictions out of 156 alleged abuse cases involving minors, 2009–2019
cite: Conferencia del Episcopado Mexicano statement, January 2020; El Universal, 2 February 2020, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Venezuela — priests accused or convicted 2001–2022
who: Catholic Church in Venezuela
d: A 2022 Washington Post investigation found at least 10 Catholic priests accused or convicted of sexual abuse in Venezuela between 2001 and 2022, with complaints in at least eleven states. Three served little or no sentence and returned to the priesthood. The church confirmed the report's accuracy and announced an investigation.
cover: Three of the priests served little or no sentence and returned to ministry
cite: Washington Post, 2022, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Brazil — priest convictions
who: Catholic dioceses in Brazil
d: In 2005 Fr Tarcísio Tadeu Spricigo and Fr Geraldo da Consolação Machado were convicted of child molestation in Brazil. Fr Felix Barbosa Carreiro was arrested and charged in Maranhão after police found him in a hotel room with four teenage boys. No national inquiry has been held in Brazil, the country with the world's largest Catholic population.
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Latin America

n: Crimen sollicitationis — secrecy instruction (1962)
who: Holy See — Holy Office (now Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith)
d: The Holy Office instruction Crimen sollicitationis, approved by Pope John XXIII on 16 March 1962 and restating a 1922 instruction, governed canonical cases of solicitation in confession and also obscene acts with pre-adolescent children. It required absolute secrecy under pain of automatic excommunication. Many bishops did not know it was in their archives until press reports in 2003. Canon lawyer Thomas Doyle called the secrecy rules 'an explicit written policy to cover up cases', while others argue it did not bar reporting to police. It stayed in force until 2001.
cover: Church proceedings to be kept absolutely confidential under automatic excommunication, binding tribunal members, accusers and witnesses
cite: Holy Office, Instructio de modo procedendi in causis sollicitationis, 1962, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela / De delictis gravioribus (2001)
who: Holy See — Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, prefect)
d: Pope John Paul II's motu proprio Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela (30 April 2001), with the CDF letter De delictis gravioribus of 18 May 2001, classed sexual abuse of a minor by a cleric as a graver delict and required that cases be sent to the CDF, then led by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger. Cases were handled under pontifical secret until December 2019. The Holy See told the UN Committee against Torture in 2014 that 3,420 abuse cases had been investigated in the previous decade and 884 priests removed.
cover: All abuse-of-minor cases reserved to the CDF under pontifical secret
cite: Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela, 30 April 2001; Holy See to UN Committee against Torture, 2014, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Benedict XVI Pastoral Letter to the Catholics of Ireland (2010)
who: Pope Benedict XVI
d: In March 2010, after the Ryan and Murphy reports, Pope Benedict XVI issued a pastoral letter to Irish Catholics addressed in part to abuse survivors, acknowledging that nothing could undo the harm done to them. Critics said it did not address systemic failures. Benedict said in 2010 that about 400 priests had been laicised over a two-year period.
cite: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Father Pope Benedict XVI to the Catholics of Ireland, 19 March 2010, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child — Holy See review (2014)
who: Holy See
d: In February 2014 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the Holy See had not taken sufficient measures against clerical abuse and had adopted practices that led to impunity. It said abusers were often moved to other parishes or countries without police being told, that bishops were not obliged to report to civil authorities, and that a code of silence meant cases were 'hardly ever reported'. In 2013 the committee had asked the Holy See for abuse data.
cover: Committee found abusive clergy were reassigned without police notification, bishops not required to report to civil authorities, and a code of silence
cite: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, Concluding observations on the second periodic report of the Holy See, CRC/C/VAT/CO/2, February 2014, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Pope Francis' letter to Chile's bishops and the Scicluna mission (2018)
who: Pope Francis; Archbishop Charles Scicluna; Mgr Jordi Bertomeu
d: After defending Bishop Juan Barros in January 2018, Pope Francis sent Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Jordi Bertomeu to take testimony in New York and Chile in February 2018. In a letter of 8 April 2018 he wrote that he had made 'serious mistakes in the assessment and perception of the situation' and summoned the Chilean bishops to Rome, where all of them offered to resign in May 2018.
cite: Pope Francis, Letter to the Bishops of Chile, 8 April 2018, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Vos estis lux mundi (2019) and February 2019 summit
who: Pope Francis
d: Three months after a February 2019 Vatican summit of bishops' conference presidents on abuse, Pope Francis signed Vos estis lux mundi on 7 May 2019. It requires clerics and religious to report suspected abuse and cover-ups to church authorities and lets bishops be investigated for cover-up, but does not require reporting to civil authorities. It was made permanent on 30 April 2023.
cite: Apostolic letter motu proprio Vos estis lux mundi, 7 May 2019, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Pontifical secret lifted for abuse cases (December 2019)
who: Pope Francis
d: On 17 December 2019 Pope Francis issued the instruction 'On the confidentiality of legal proceedings', removing the pontifical secret from cases of sexual abuse of minors and vulnerable persons, child sexual abuse material involving under-18s, and concealment of such crimes. Documents remain non-public but may be shared with civil authorities with jurisdiction.
cite: Rescriptum ex audientia, 17 December 2019, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: McCarrick Report (Holy See, November 2020)
who: Holy See; former Cardinal Theodore McCarrick
d: The Holy See's report of 10 November 2020 found that Pope John Paul II learned of allegations against Theodore McCarrick through a 1999 letter from Cardinal O'Connor but appointed him Archbishop of Washington after McCarrick denied them in writing. It faulted Benedict XVI for not stopping his influence and said Francis learned of allegations involving minors only in 2018. McCarrick was found guilty by the CDF and laicised on 16 February 2019. A Massachusetts charge of assaulting a 16-year-old in 1974 did not go to trial after he was ruled incompetent in 2023; he died in April 2025.
cover: A 1999 warning letter reached Pope John Paul II; an inquiry stalled after three of four US bishops gave 'inaccurate and incomplete information'; McCarrick was promoted to Washington in 2000
cite: Secretariat of State, Report on the Holy See's Institutional Knowledge and Decision-Making Related to Former Cardinal Theodore Edgar McCarrick, 10 November 2020

n: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
d: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in August 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors; Dominican authorities opened an investigation in September 2013. The Vatican laicised him in June 2014 and indicted him in June 2015 for possessing child abuse images, but he died on 27 August 2015 before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, who worked at the nunciature, returned to Poland; using Dominican evidence, Polish police arrested him in February 2014 and he was sentenced to seven years in March 2015.
cover: Wesołowski recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic
cite: Wikipedia, Józef Wesołowski, citing Vatican and Dominican statements and Polish court reporting

n: Vatican tribunal — diplomat Carlo Capella and the Martinelli trial
who: Holy See diplomat Mgr Carlo Capella; St Pius X pre-seminary
d: On 23 June 2018 a Vatican City court convicted former Holy See diplomat Carlo Capella, recalled from the Washington nunciature, of possessing child abuse images and sentenced him to five years. On 14 October 2020 the first Vatican criminal trial for sexual abuse began, of Fr Gabriele Martinelli over abuse at the pre-seminary for altar boys inside the Vatican, with a former rector charged with aiding and abetting.
cite: Vatican City State tribunal, 23 June 2018; Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases by country

n: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
d: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused at least 143 children over more than 40 years in Belfast, Dublin and the United States (Rhode Island, North Dakota, Boston). In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, witnessed two boys sign oaths of silence during a church inquiry; police were not told. After his 1991 arrest he hid in the Republic for three years; the handling of the RUC's extradition request contributed to the collapse of the Irish government in December 1994. He was convicted in Belfast in 1994 and in Dublin in 1997 (74 counts, 12 years) and died in prison in August 1997.
cover: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994
cite: Wikipedia, Brendan Smyth, citing court records and Irish press

n: Diocese of Raphoe — Fr Eugene Greene
who: Catholic Diocese of Raphoe
d: While Séamus Hegarty was Bishop of Raphoe (1982–1994), Fr Eugene Greene raped 26 young people. Greene was arrested in 1999 and in 2000 pleaded guilty to 40 of 115 charges, receiving 12 years. Four more Raphoe priests were convicted of sex abuse in 2011.
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Ireland

n: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland — review 2020
who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (with Scout Association of Ireland), now Scouting Ireland
d: A review published in May 2020 found that over several decades before their 2004 merger into Scouting Ireland, the Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland and the Scout Association of Ireland shielded 275 known or suspected abusers. Scouting Ireland accepted the findings and apologised.
cover: Organisations shielded known or suspected abusers after abuse was reported
cite: Scouting Ireland historical abuse review, May 2020, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Sisters of Nazareth
who: Poor Sisters of Nazareth
d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry found in May 2019 that children in Nazareth House orphanages from 1933 to 1984 suffered sexual abuse 'of the utmost depravity'. Police received more than 300 complaints. In 2025 the Sisters agreed to pay up to £5.75 million to survivors and three former staff were convicted.
cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 2 findings (Nazareth Houses), 2019

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Smyllum Park and Bellevue (Daughters of Charity)
who: Daughters of Charity of St Vincent de Paul
d: About 11,600 children passed through Smyllum Park orphanage, run by the Daughters of Charity from 1864 to 1981. The inquiry's October 2018 findings said children were sexually abused by priests, a trainee priest, sisters, staff and a volunteer, and beaten with implements. Seventeen people were later charged; in 2025 the order agreed to pay up to £10 million.
cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 1 findings (Daughters of Charity), October 2018

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Fort Augustus Abbey and Carlekemp (Benedictines)
who: English Benedictine Congregation — Fort Augustus Abbey School and Carlekemp Priory School
d: In August 2021 the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry found both Benedictine schools were 'havens for paedophiles' with sexual abuse over many years. A 2013 BBC programme had presented evidence against seven monks. Denis Chrysostom Alexander, sent back to Australia after parents complained, was arrested in Sydney in 2017 and pleaded guilty in 2021; Robert MacKenzie was extradited from Canada in 2020 but the case was dropped in 2021.
cover: Complaints to senior monks were inadequately handled; after one complaint the school did not tell police and sent the monk, Denis Chrysostom Alexander, back to Australia
cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study findings on Benedictine establishments, August 2021; BBC Scotland 'Sins of Our Fathers' 2013

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Marist and Christian Brothers schools
who: Marist Brothers (St Joseph's College Dumfries, St Columba's College Largs); Christian Brothers (St Ninian's, Falkland)
d: The inquiry found in February 2021 that the Christian Brothers' St Ninian's school in Falkland was 'a place of abuse and deprivation', especially 1969–1983; two Brothers were jailed in 2016 for abuse of 35 boys across more than 100 charges. It found abuse at the Marist Brothers' schools in Dumfries and Largs between 1951 and 1980 'shocking and distressing'; the Marists apologised in November 2021.
cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, findings on Christian Brothers (Feb 2021) and Marist Brothers (2021)

n: Fr Paul Moore — moved by his bishop to Toronto
who: Diocese of Galloway; Bishop Maurice Taylor
d: Fr Paul Moore was convicted in 2018 of abusing three children between 1977 and 1981 and a student priest in 1995. Bishop Maurice Taylor had sent him to Toronto, Canada and to Fort Augustus.
cover: Bishop Maurice Taylor sent Moore to Toronto and Fort Augustus
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases by country (Scotland), citing BBC

n: Indian Residential Schools run by Catholic entities — TRC and papal apology
who: Catholic dioceses and orders (incl. Oblates of Mary Immaculate) that ran about 44 of 80 schools at the 1931 peak (TRC says about 70% overall)
d: About 150,000 Indigenous children were sent to Canada's residential schools; at the 1931 peak 44 of 80 were run by Catholic dioceses and orders. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's 2015 report called the system cultural genocide; the Independent Assessment Process resolved 31,970 claims of sexual or serious physical assault. Oblates faced more than 2,000 lawsuits in western provinces. In July 2022 Pope Francis apologised at Maskwacis for 'the evil committed by so many Christians'.
cover: Federal government funded and mandated attendance; Catholic entities cited lack of funds to compensate
cite: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, Final Report, December 2015; Wikipedia, Canadian Indian residential school system

n: Basilian Fathers — Canadian convictions
who: Congregation of St. Basil (Basilian Fathers)
d: Basilian priest William Hodgson Marshall pleaded guilty in 2011 to 16 counts of indecent assault and one of sexual assault from 1952–1986 in Windsor, Toronto and Sudbury schools. Robert Whyte pleaded guilty in 1990 to abusing 18 children (1962–1982); Kenneth O'Keefe received house arrest in 2012–2013. In April 2020 the Supreme Court of Canada let stand an award of over $2.5 million, including $500,000 punitive damages, against the Basilians.
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Canada, citing court rulings

n: Fr Eric Dejaeger — Oblate in Nunavut
who: Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate; Belgian-born Fr Eric Dejaeger
d: Belgian-born Oblate Eric Dejaeger was convicted on 12 September 2014 of 24 counts of indecent assault and other sexual offences against Inuit children in Igloolik, Nunavut, between 1978 and 1982. He had earlier been convicted of 11 counts of sexual and indecent assault against children at his previous post in Baker Lake.
cite: Nunavut Court of Justice, 2014, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Archdiocese of Los Angeles — settlements 2007 and 2024
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Los Angeles; Cardinal Roger Mahony
d: The Archdiocese of Los Angeles agreed a $660 million settlement with 508 victims in 2007 and, in October 2024, an $880 million settlement with 1,350 victims, the largest by any US diocese; total payouts reached about $1.5 billion. In February 2013 Archbishop José Gómez barred Cardinal Roger Mahony from public ministry over his handling of abusers.
cover: In 2013 Archbishop Gómez removed Cardinal Mahony from public duties over his handling of abusive clergy
cite: Wikipedia, Sexual abuse scandal in the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Los Angeles

n: Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady
who: Diocese of Stockton; Bishop Roger Mahony (later Cardinal Archbishop of Los Angeles)
d: Irish-born priest Oliver O'Grady, ordained in 1971 for the Diocese of Stockton, abused children from about 1973 and was moved between parishes. Bishop Roger Mahony knew of concerns by 1980 and moved him in 1984. O'Grady was convicted in 1993 and sentenced to 14 years; a 1998 civil jury awarded $30 million (reduced to $7 million). Paroled and deported to Ireland in 2000, he was convicted there for child abuse images in 2012 and 2020.
cover: Bishop Mahony ordered him away from one family in 1980, then moved him to a new parish in 1984 before a psychiatric evaluation was complete
cite: Wikipedia, Oliver O'Grady, citing court records

n: Diocese of Lafayette — Gilbert Gauthe (first national case)
who: Diocese of Lafayette; Fr Gilbert Gauthe
d: Fr Gilbert Gauthe admitted abusing 37 children while serving in the Diocese of Lafayette from 1972 to 1983. In 1974 the bishop made him a Boy Scout chaplain despite allegations about altar boys. In October 1985 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 20 years; the diocese paid more than $20 million. His 1984–85 case was the first widely publicised clergy abuse prosecution in the US.
cover: Bishop assigned him as Boy Scout chaplain in 1974 despite allegations; sent for therapy in 1976 and returned
cite: Wikipedia, Gilbert Gauthe

n: US diocesan bankruptcies and settlements
who: US Catholic dioceses (Portland, Tucson, Spokane, San Diego, Davenport, Milwaukee, Albany and others)
d: Starting with Portland in 2004, at least 13 US dioceses filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy by 2023 under abuse claims. US dioceses have paid about $4 billion to roughly 17,000 victims since the 1980s. In Milwaukee, which filed in 2011 after paying $29 million on about 200 cases, released documents showed abusive priests were moved between assignments without notifying law enforcement.
cover: Milwaukee: Cardinal Timothy Dolan, with Vatican approval, moved $57 million into a cemetery trust, which kept it from victims; released files showed priests moved without telling police
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic sexual abuse scandal in the United States

n: Christian Brothers in Australia — Ballarat and WA orphanages
who: Congregation of Christian Brothers
d: The Royal Commission found 22% of Christian Brothers in Australia had been alleged perpetrators since 1950, and that claims concerning 853 children, against 281 Brothers, led to A$37.3 million in compensation. In Ballarat Brothers Best and Dowlan were moved between campuses and kept offending. From 1980 to 2015 the Christian Brothers made 763 payments totalling A$48.5 million, the most of any Catholic authority. Over 200 former residents of the WA orphanages, including child migrants, sued from 1993 and settled in 1996.
cover: Convicted Brothers Dowlan and Best were moved from junior to senior campus and continued offending; leaders knew of abuse at WA orphanages for decades
cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, final report Dec 2017; Wikipedia, Congregation of Christian Brothers

n: Maitland-Newcastle diocese — Fletcher, Cunneen inquiry and Archbishop Wilson (acquitted)
who: Diocese of Maitland-Newcastle; Archbishop Philip Wilson
d: A NSW Special Commission of Inquiry led by Margaret Cunneen, ordered in November 2012, reported on 30 May 2014 on church and police handling of abuse in the diocese; police Strike Force Lantle laid more than 170 charges. Archbishop of Adelaide Philip Wilson was found guilty on 22 May 2018 of failing to report abuse by Fr James Fletcher in 1976, but was acquitted on appeal on 6 December 2018. Fletcher died in jail in 2006.
cover: Monsignor Cotter's letter about Fr Denis McAlinden said 'we do not think it can be real serious'
cite: Special Commission of Inquiry into matters relating to the Police investigation of certain child sexual abuse allegations in the Catholic Diocese of Maitland-Newcastle, 30 May 2014; NSW District Court 6 Dec 2018

n: Marist Brothers in Australia
who: Marist Brothers
d: In June 2019 the Marist Brothers listed 154 members accused of abusing children in Australia between 1980 and 2015. The Royal Commission found the order's response worsened the harm and that many alleged abusers kept access to children for years. Brother William Wade was convicted in 2017 of abusing two boys and in 2020 pleaded guilty to concealing abuse.
cover: Royal Commission found the order failed to act on complaints against a Brother at Marist College Ashgrove; a Brother pleaded guilty in 2020 to concealing abuse
cite: Marist Brothers statement, June 2019; Royal Commission findings, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Marylands School and Hebron Trust — St John of God Brothers
who: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God
d: Marylands, a Christchurch residential school for boys with learning disabilities run by the St John of God Brothers from 1955 to 1984, and the order's later Hebron Trust, were described by the Royal Commission in 2023 as 'hell on earth'. 21 of the 37 Brothers who served in Christchurch faced abuse allegations. Bernard McGrath, known to have offended from 1977, was convicted in NZ in 1993 and 2006 and extradited to Australia in 2014 to face 252 charges. The order's Australasian branch had paid NZ$5.1 million by 2006.
cover: Brother Bernard McGrath was transferred to Australia after 1977 allegations and later put in charge of Hebron Trust; victims sometimes required to sign non-disclosure agreements
cite: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, 'Stolen Lives, Marked Souls', July 2023; Wikipedia, Marylands School

n: Marist Brothers and priests — New Zealand convictions
who: Marist Brothers; Society of Mary
d: A 2018 Otago Daily Times report listed nine Marist Brothers convicted of crimes against boys in New Zealand, including two at Hato Paora College. Marist priest Alan Woodcock was extradited from England and convicted in 2004 of 21 offences (1978–1987). Brother Kevin Healy was convicted in 2020. The church admitted in 2022 that 14% of its diocesan clergy had been accused since 1950.
cite: Otago Daily Times 2018 and court reports, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Fiji — transferred clergy and Julian Fox
who: Salesians; Catholic Church in Fiji
d: Salesian priest Julian Fox was moved to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating abuse allegations; he was jailed in Australia in 2015. The Catholic Church in Fiji knew of the allegations nine years before he was charged. In July 2020 1News reported that some of about 1,300 alleged child abuse cases involving clergy in Fiji concerned clergy from Australia and New Zealand.
cover: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating; the Fiji church knew of allegations nine years before he was charged
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Australia and New Zealand, citing 1News (July 2020)

n: Richard Daschbach — Topu Honis shelter, Oecusse
who: Society of the Divine Word (SVD); US-born Fr Richard Daschbach
d: US-born Divine Word missionary Richard Daschbach founded the Topu Honis children's shelter in Oecusse in 1991 and admitted abusing minors there between 1991 and 2012. The Vatican dismissed him from the priesthood (2018–2020). Timor-Leste prosecutors charged him with 14 counts in September 2020, and on 21 December 2021 a court convicted him of abusing four girls and sentenced him to 12 years. A 2020 Diocese of Dili report had disputed the allegations.
cite: Oecusse District Court, 21 December 2021, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo — Vatican sanctions
who: Salesians; Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo (Nobel Peace laureate)
d: On 28 September 2022 Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer reported that two men said Bishop Belo had abused them and other boys in Fatumaca and Dili, before and during his time as bishop. The next day the Vatican confirmed it had received allegations in 2019 and imposed disciplinary sanctions in 2020: limits on movement and ministry, no contact with minors and no contact with Timor-Leste. The sanctions were reinforced in 2021. Belo had left Timor in 2002 and worked in Maputo, Mozambique from 2004.
cover: Vatican received allegations in 2019 and imposed sanctions in 2020 but did not disclose them until a magazine reported the case in 2022
cite: De Groene Amsterdammer, 28 September 2022; Holy See Press Office statement, 29 September 2022, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Kerala — priest convictions and Bishop Mulakkal acquittal
who: Syro-Malabar and Latin dioceses in Kerala; Bishop Franco Mulakkal of Jalandhar
d: Fr Robin Vadakkumchery of Kannur was arrested in 2017 for raping a 15-year-old girl who later gave birth, and was sentenced to 20 years by a POCSO court in 2019. In 2014 Fr Raju Kokkan of Thrissur was arrested for raping a nine-year-old, and three other Kerala priests were arrested on charges of raping minors. Bishop Franco Mulakkal, accused by an adult nun of rape between 2014 and 2016, was arrested on 21 September 2018 and acquitted of all charges on 14 January 2022; he resigned in 2023. In 2016 the Ootacamund diocese reappointed a convicted priest without safeguards.
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Asia; Franco Mulakkal

n: Philippines — priest arrests and removals
who: Catholic dioceses in the Philippines; a US priest assigned in Biliran
d: In 2018 an American priest assigned in the Philippines was arrested for abusing at least 10 boys in Naval, Biliran. Other cases include a priest arrested in Marikina (2017), a priest charged in Cadiz City with raping a four-year-old (2019), an arrest in Tuguegarao for abusing a 16-year-old (2022), and a Diocese of San Carlos priest arrested in March 2023 for raping a 17-year-old choir member. Pope Francis removed a Borongan priest on 10 May 2023. There has been no national inquiry in Asia's largest Catholic country.
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Asia, citing Philippine press

n: Indonesia — Syahril Parlindungan Marbun, altar boys
who: Catholic parish (church volunteer Syahril Parlindungan Marbun)
d: Police reported that Syahril Parlindungan Marbun abused 20 altar boys between 2002 and 2020, and said the number could be higher.
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Asia, citing Indonesian police statements

n: St Michael's School, Soni — Rosminian priests
who: Institute of Charity (Rosminians); English priest Kit Cunningham and three others
d: In the 1960s English Rosminian priest Kit Cunningham and three other priests abused boys at St Michael's boarding school in Soni, Tanzania. The order knew before Cunningham's death in 2010; the abuse became public in a BBC documentary on 21 June 2011. Former pupils sued in Leicester in March 2013, and the order's 2014–15 accounts show £1,746,523 in settlement and legal costs; it later apologised for the abuse and cover-up.
cover: The order knew of Cunningham's abuse before his death in 2010; it became public only through a BBC documentary in June 2011
cite: BBC, 'Abused: Breaking the Silence', 21 June 2011; Rosminian charity accounts 2015, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Kenya — RTÉ 'Mission to Prey' and false allegation against Fr Kevin Reynolds
who: Irish missionaries in Kenya; RTÉ
d: RTÉ's May 2011 documentary 'Mission to Prey' reported on clerical abuse by missionaries in Africa. It wrongly alleged that Irish priest Fr Kevin Reynolds had abused a girl and fathered a child in Kenya; paternity tests disproved this and RTÉ apologised and paid damages, a major Irish broadcasting scandal. Separately in 2011 a Dutch bishop was investigated over alleged abuse of a minor 18 years earlier when he was a priest in Ngong diocese, and was retired by the church.
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Africa, citing RTÉ

n: Mauritius — Irish missionary abuse and priest convictions
who: Catholic Diocese of Port Louis; Irish priest at St Joseph's College
d: A survivor has said he was abused at age 11 in the late 1950s by an Irish priest at St Joseph's College, Curepipe. In October 2019 Fr Joseph-Marie Moctee was sentenced to three years for abusing a 15-year-old in April 2015 at Chamarel. In September 2016 another priest was arrested over a complaint at St Louis Cathedral, Port Louis (complainant aged 20).
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Africa, citing Mauritian press

n: Slovenia — Fr Franc Frantar
who: Archdiocese of Ljubljana; Fr Franc Frantar
d: Slovenian priest Franc Frantar was detained in 2006 for abusing up to 16 minors and later sentenced (sources give three and a half and five years). He first avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary and returned to Slovenia after Interpol issued a notice.
cover: Avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary until an Interpol notice was issued
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe

n: Croatia — first priest convictions
who: Catholic dioceses in Croatia
d: In 2000 Fr Ivan Čuček was convicted of abusing 37 girls; his three-year sentence was cut to 18 months by the Supreme Court. In 2007 Fr Drago Ljubičić of Rab became the first Croatian priest to serve prison time, three years for molesting five teenage boys. Fr Nediljko Ivanov of Bibinje became the first priest convicted by a Croatian church court, but civil prosecution was time-barred.
cover: Nediljko Ivanov, whose abuse 1983–1991 was reported in 2012, was time-barred; a church court ordered only prayer, fasting and an apology and he continued to say Mass
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe and by country

n: Czech Republic — Fr František Merta
who: Archdiocese of Olomouc; Archbishop Jan Graubner (alleged failure to report)
d: In 2000–2001 Fr František Merta was found guilty of abusing more than 20 boys and received a two-year suspended sentence. Archbishop Jan Graubner allegedly failed to report him and moved him between parishes when problems arose.
cover: Archbishop Graubner allegedly did not report him and moved him between parishes
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe

n: Norway — Bishop Georg Müller of Trondheim
who: Territorial Prelature of Trondheim; Bishop Georg Müller
d: Former Bishop of Trondheim Georg Müller, who retired in 2009, admitted in 2010 that he had abused an altar boy in the 1980s. In April 2010 the church in Norway had reported 18 abuse cases; in Denmark 17 had been reported.
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe

n: Malta — St Joseph Home convictions
who: Missionary Society of St Paul (St Joseph Home); Maltese clergy
d: By April 2010 the church in Malta had recorded 84 allegations. Fr Charles Pulis was sentenced to six years and Fr Godwin Scerri to five years for abusing boys at a church children's home; Donald Bellizzi received three years in 2020.
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases by country (Malta)

n: Belgium — Halsberghe commission (2000) and convictions
who: Catholic Church in Belgium
d: A church commission chaired by Godelieve Halsberghe from 2000 received over 300 complaints and upheld 32 of 33 formal ones; 31 were time-barred. Convictions included Fr Bruno Vos (nine years in 2009 for raping four minors), Robert Borremans (five years, 2008) and two Brothers jailed for ten years each in 2005 for abusing disabled people. On 24 June 2010 police raided the archbishop's palace in Mechelen, seizing 450 dossiers, and searched Cardinal Danneels' residence.
cover: In about half the 32 upheld cases the accused refused to appear; 31 cases were time-barred and only one reached court; in June 2010 police seized 450 internal dossiers from the Mechelen archbishop's palace
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Belgium

n: Italy — no national inquiry; Rete l'Abuso count
who: Catholic Church in Italy; Italian Bishops' Conference
d: Italy has no official statistics or national inquiry. The victims' network Rete l'Abuso counted about 300 cases of priests and nuns before Italian courts since 2000, with 150 to 170 convictions (October 2018). In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference said its priests had no duty to report suspected abuse to police. Cases include Fr Mauro Galli (6 years 4 months, 2014) and a former Roman Rota judge who pleaded guilty to child abuse image offences in 2018.
cover: In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference said priests had no obligation to report suspected abuse to police
cite: Rete l'Abuso, 2018; Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Italy

n: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta of Orán — convicted 2022
who: Diocese of Orán; Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
d: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta resigned from the Diocese of Orán in August 2017 amid complaints from clergy and was named an official at the Vatican's patrimony office (APSA) in December 2017. Argentine prosecutors charged him in June 2019 with sexually abusing two adult seminarians, and on 4 March 2022 a Salta court sentenced him to four and a half years. Included as a case of a bishop moved to the Vatican, though the victims were adults.
cover: After resigning in 2017 amid complaints he was given a post at the Vatican's APSA in December 2017; suspended in January 2019
cite: Salta court verdict, 4 March 2022, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Chile — Fr José Andrés Aguirre ('Cura Tato')
who: Archdiocese of Santiago
d: Fr José Andrés Aguirre Ovalle, known as 'Cura Tato', was found guilty of nine sexual abuse charges and sentenced to 12 years. A lower-court order for the church to pay damages was revoked by the Supreme Court. Chile removed the statute of limitations for child sexual abuse on 11 July 2019 (not retroactive).
cite: Chilean court rulings, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Denis Chrysostom Alexander — extradition from Australia
who: Benedictine monk, Fort Augustus Abbey School
d: Benedictine monk Denis 'Chrysostom' Alexander abused pupils at Fort Augustus Abbey School in Scotland; after a pupil's parents complained, the school sent him back to Australia without informing police. He was arrested in Sydney in 2017, extradition was approved in 2019, and in June 2021 he pleaded guilty to two charges involving two boys between 1973 and 1976.
cover: Sent back to Australia by the school after parents complained; police not informed
cite: Wikipedia, Fort Augustus Abbey, citing BBC

n: Sodalicio layman arrested with a boy, Lima 2007
who: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (consecrated layman)
d: In 2007 Daniel Bernardo Beltrán Murguía Ward, a consecrated layman of the Sodalitium, was found in a Lima hostel photographing an 11-year-old boy; police reported photos of two other boys on his camera. He denied the charges and was removed from the group.
cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Latin America, citing Peruvian press

n: Conti v. Watchtower — Fremont congregation, California
who: Watchtower Bible and Tract Society (Jehovah's Witnesses)
d: In June 2012 an Alameda County jury found the Watchtower Society liable for abuse of a girl by a congregation member and awarded punitive damages, later reduced. In April 2015 the California appeals court reversed punitive damages but upheld $2.8 million in compensatory damages; the case settled during further appeal. Other US civil cases followed, including a $13.5 million San Diego judgment in 2014 (vacated 2016, settled 2018) and a $35 million Montana verdict in 2018 reversed in 2020.
cite: Doe (Conti) v. Watchtower, California Court of Appeal, April 2015 (summarised in Wikipedia with citations)

n: A v Watchtower — High Court damages over Peter Stewart abuse
who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain
d: On 19 June 2015 the High Court awarded £275,000 damages to a woman abused as a child by Jehovah's Witness ministerial servant Peter Stewart, holding the organisation liable; appeals were refused. In a separate 2014 case in Barry, Wales, elder Mark Sewell was sentenced to 14 years for eight sex offences, and most of the investigating elders declined to give evidence.
cite: A v Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, High Court, 19 June 2015 (summarised in Wikipedia with citations)

n: Re ST (A Minor) — High Court judgment on The Family (Children of God)
who: The Family / Children of God (now The Family International)
d: In a custody case decided on 19 October 1995 after three years of hearings, Lord Justice Alan Ward found that the group, including some top leaders, had in the past sexually abused minors and used severe corporal punishment and sequestration of children. He found these practices had been abandoned by 1995, let the mother keep custody, and required the group to end corporal punishment in the UK and to denounce founder David Berg's writings that had led to children being subjected to sexually inappropriate behaviour. A 2005 group spokesperson acknowledged 'sexually inappropriate advances' in a 1978–1986 transitional period.
cite: Re ST (A Minor), judgment of Lord Justice Ward, 19 October 1995 (summarised by CESNUR, International Journal of Cultic Studies, and Wikipedia)

n: Asaram Bapu — convicted of raping a 16-year-old at his ashram
who: Asaram Bapu ashrams
d: A 16-year-old girl said guru Asaram Bapu assaulted her on 15 August 2013 at his Manai ashram; he was arrested by Jodhpur police on 1 September 2013. On 25 April 2018 a Jodhpur court convicted him of raping a minor and sentenced him to life imprisonment. In January 2023 a Gandhinagar court gave him a second life term in a case brought by two sisters from Surat.
cover: Witnesses in his cases were attacked; a former aide was shot dead in May 2014 and the key witness in the Surat case was shot dead in January 2015.
cite: Jodhpur SC/ST court judgment, 25 April 2018 (via Wikipedia 'Asaram' with citations)

n: Nithyananda — Gujarat abduction case and flight from India
who: Nithyananda Dhyanapeetam
d: On 17 November 2019 Gujarat Police registered a case of abduction after a Tamil Nadu couple said three of their children had been taken from Bangalore to Nithyananda's Ahmedabad ashram without consent. Police said on 20 November 2019 that Nithyananda had fled India after skipping hearings, and by January 2020 Interpol had issued a blue corner notice to locate him; he claims to have founded a 'Hindu nation', Kailasa. On 2 February 2024 the Gujarat High Court dismissed the father's habeas corpus petition, finding the daughters were adults who chose to stay with the group. He separately faces a 2010 rape case brought by an adult disciple.
cite: The Hindu, 21 November 2019; NDTV, 22 January 2020; Indian Express, 3 February 2024 (via Wikipedia 'Nithyananda')

n: Manitoba Colony 'ghost rapes' — Mennonite colony, Bolivia
who: Old Colony Mennonite community, Manitoba Colony
d: Between 2005 and 2009 men from the Manitoba Mennonite Colony sedated households with an animal anaesthetic spray and raped women and girls, the youngest three years old. In August 2011 a Bolivian court sentenced seven men to 25 years each; a veterinarian from a neighbouring colony who supplied the sedative got 12 years.
cover: The attacks were first blamed on ghosts or demons; a 2013 investigation reported similar assaults continuing.
cite: TIME, 26 August 2011; BBC News, 16 May 2019 (via Wikipedia 'Manitoba Colony, Bolivia')

n: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane — Archbishop Peter Hollingworth's handling of abuse
who: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane; Toowoomba Preparatory School; Church of England Boys' Society
d: In 2001 the Diocese of Brisbane was ordered to pay A$834,800 to a victim of a teacher at Toowoomba Preparatory School, and Hollingworth, archbishop 1989–2001, was accused of mishandling the complaint. A report commissioned by his successor was tabled in the Queensland parliament in May 2003; it found he had let a known abuser continue as a priest in 1993. Hollingworth resigned as Governor-General on 26 May 2003, and at the Royal Commission in 2016 apologised for not pursuing claims more rigorously.
cover: A diocesan inquiry found that in 1993 Archbishop Hollingworth allowed a known paedophile to keep working as a priest. He later became Governor-General of Australia.
cite: Diocese of Brisbane report tabled in Queensland Parliament, May 2003; ABC, BBC, The Age, May 2003 (via Wikipedia 'Peter Hollingworth')

n: Salvation Army boys' homes — Australia
who: The Salvation Army (Australia)
d: The Salvation Army sheltered about 30,000 Australian children from the 1940s to the 1980s and apologised in 2006 for abuse that may have occurred. Private settlements totalling A$15.5 million for 474 cases in Victoria were reported in 2013. In January–February 2014 the Royal Commission's Case Study 5 examined abuse at Bexley Boys' Home, Gill Memorial Home (Goulburn), Alkira (Indooroopilly) and Riverview Training Farm, and how accused officers were investigated and transferred.
cover: The Royal Commission heard that officers accused of abuse were moved interstate.
cite: Royal Commission Case Studies 5, 10 and 33 (2014–2015); Wikipedia 'The Salvation Army' (index)

n: Rev. Gordon Nakayama — Anglican dioceses of New Westminster and Calgary
who: Anglican Church of Canada; Japanese Canadian congregations
d: Gordon Nakayama, a priest serving Japanese Canadian communities, abused over 300 children during 62 years of ministry. Bishop Barry Curtis charged him with immorality in 1994 after a written confession, but police were not told. In 2015 the two dioceses jointly apologised for not reporting, and in 2021 the Anglican Church of Canada and the National Association of Japanese Canadians set up a $610,000 healing fund.
cover: Nakayama made a written confession in 1994; the dioceses did not report it to police. He was allowed to resign and died in 1995.
cite: Anglican Journal, 17 June 2015; Bulletin/Geppo, April 2021 (via Wikipedia 'Anglican Communion sexual abuse cases')

n: Terry Knight — Diocese of Portsmouth
who: Church of England, Diocese of Portsmouth
d: Terry Knight, active in the Diocese of Portsmouth, was convicted of child sexual offences in 1996 and again in 2016. Parents had raised concerns with the bishop in 1985, who did not inform police.
cover: Bishop Timothy Bavin did not report Knight to police when parents raised concerns in 1985.
cite: The News (Portsmouth), 2015–2016 (via Wikipedia 'Anglican Communion sexual abuse cases')

n: Dilworth School — Anglican boarding school, Auckland
who: Dilworth Trust (Anglican-linked school for boys from disadvantaged families)
d: Police Operation Beverly arrested six men on 14 September 2020 over historic offences at Dilworth from the 1970s to the early 2000s; by June 2021 eleven men had been charged, including a former chaplain who pleaded guilty to abusing 16 boys. Twelve former staff were prosecuted. An independent inquiry by Silvia Cartwright and Frances Joychild, released 18 September 2023, covered 1950–2005 and recorded 175 reports of sexual abuse and 134 of serious physical abuse. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care also examined Dilworth.
cover: The independent inquiry concluded that ongoing silence about the abuse was 'the primary reason for the damage' to former students.
cite: Cartwright & Joychild, Dilworth independent inquiry report, 18 September 2023; RNZ, Stuff, NZ Herald 2020–2023 (via Wikipedia 'Dilworth School')

n: Gloriavale Christian Community — convictions and Employment Court findings
who: Gloriavale Christian Community
d: Founder Neville 'Hopeful Christian' Cooper was convicted in 1995 of sexual abuse of young members and jailed for five years. Police and Oranga Tamariki launched Operation Minneapolis in 2020; a former member was sentenced in March 2024 to 11 years 10 months for 26 child sexual offences, and leader Howard Temple pleaded guilty in 2025 to 12 charges involving girls. In May 2022 the Employment Court ruled in Courage v Gloriavale that three former members had been employees from age six, doing dangerous work.
cover: In January 2025 Gloriavale's leadership said past leaders had not reported known abuse to authorities; in 2026 the Charities Registration Board cited the school's failure to report child sexual offending.
cite: Employment Court, Courage v Attorney-General/Gloriavale (May 2022, July 2023); RNZ, Stuff (via Wikipedia 'Gloriavale Christian Community')

n: Jesus Fellowship (Jesus Army) — Operation Lifeboat and redress scheme
who: Jesus Fellowship Church / Jesus Fellowship Community Trust
d: After founder Noel Stanton died in 2009, Northamptonshire Police ran Operation Lifeboat into historic abuse; about ten to twelve former members were convicted of sex offences. The church's redress scheme, whose final report was published on 11 September 2024, received 601 applications, paid £7.7 million, identified 539 alleged perpetrators and accepted responsibility for 264 of them, 61% of whom were former leaders.
cite: Jesus Fellowship Redress Scheme Final Report, 11 September 2024; BBC News 2019–2024 (via Wikipedia 'Jesus Army')

n: Independent Fundamental Baptist churches — Star-Telegram investigation
who: Independent Fundamental Baptist churches and institutions
d: A 2018 Fort Worth Star-Telegram investigation identified 412 allegations of sexual misconduct in 187 Independent Fundamental Baptist churches and institutions across the US and Canada, some dating back to the 1970s, and described leaders moving accused men between churches.
cite: Fort Worth Star-Telegram, December 2018 (via Wikipedia 'Independent Fundamental Baptist')

n: Jack Schaap — First Baptist Church of Hammond, Indiana
who: First Baptist Church of Hammond / Hyles-Anderson College (IFB)
d: Jack Schaap, pastor of one of the largest IFB churches, was charged in September 2012 with taking a 16-year-old girl across state lines for sex (Mann Act), pleaded guilty, and was sentenced in March 2013 to 12 years in federal prison. Earlier, deacon A.V. Ballenger was jailed in 1993 for molesting a 7-year-old in Sunday school.
cite: Chicago Tribune, September 2012 and May 2022 (via Wikipedia 'First Baptist Church of Hammond')

n: Samuel Bateman — FLDS splinter group, Short Creek
who: Splinter group of the FLDS led by Samuel Bateman
d: Samuel Bateman, who claimed to succeed Warren Jeffs, took more than 20 'spiritual wives' between 2019 and 2022, at least 10 of them minors. Arizona officers stopped him in Flagstaff in August 2022 with three girls aged 11 to 14 in a trailer. He pleaded guilty on 1 April 2024 to conspiracy to transport a minor for criminal sexual activity and conspiracy to kidnap, and on 9 December 2024 was sentenced to 50 years; eleven followers were also convicted.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Arizona, December 2024 (via Wikipedia 'Samuel Bateman')

n: La Luz del Mundo — leader Naasón Joaquín García convicted
who: La Luz del Mundo church (HQ Guadalajara, Mexico)
d: Naasón Joaquín García, leader of La Luz del Mundo, was arrested at Los Angeles airport on 4 June 2019 on charges brought by the California Attorney General including forcible rape of a minor and child pornography. On 3 June 2022 he pleaded guilty to three charges related to sexually abusing children and was sentenced to 16 years 8 months. Co-defendant Alondra Ocampo pleaded guilty in October 2020 to four felony counts involving minors. In 1997 former members in Mexico had accused his father, Samuel Joaquín Flores, of abuse, but the statute of limitations had expired.
cite: California Department of Justice charges, 2019–2022; Los Angeles Times, AP, BBC (via Wikipedia 'Naasón Joaquín García' and 'La Luz del Mundo')

n: Apollo Quiboloy — Kingdom of Jesus Christ
who: Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC)
d: In November 2021 a federal grand jury in the Central District of California indicted Quiboloy and church administrators for sex trafficking, alleging girls as young as 12 were abused, and alleging followers were brought to the US and forced to solicit donations. The Philippine Department of Justice filed child abuse and human trafficking charges in March 2024, and he was taken into custody in Davao City on 8 September 2024 after police raids on the compound. He denies the charges.
cite: US indictment, C.D. Cal., November 2021; Philippine DOJ, 2024 (via Wikipedia 'Apollo Quiboloy' and 'Kingdom of Jesus Christ')

n: Global Ikhwan (GISB) children's homes — Operation Global
who: Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB), linked to the banned Al-Arqam movement
d: On 11 September 2024 Malaysian police raided 20 children's homes run by GISB and rescued 402 children aged 1 to 17; health checks found physical injuries and signs of sexual abuse. By 23 October 2024 police had made 415 arrests. Charges included sexual assault of children by madrasah teaching assistants, human trafficking, and organised-crime charges against the group's CEO; a caretaker was jailed for 10 years on 26 September 2024.
cite: Royal Malaysia Police statements, September–October 2024; The Star, Bernama, Reuters (via Wikipedia 'Global Ikhwan')

n: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
d: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leader Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner kidnapped a 14-year-old girl and 12-year-old boy from their mother, who had objected to her daughter's marriage to an older man at 13, and took them to Mexico. They were convicted in a US federal court on 10 November 2021 and sentenced to 12 years each on 31 March 2022. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.
cite: US federal court, 2021–2022 (via Wikipedia 'Lev Tahor', citing BBC, Times of Israel, court records)

n: Lev Tahor — Guatemala removal of 160 minors
who: Lev Tahor
d: In December 2024 Guatemalan authorities removed 160 minors from a Lev Tahor farm compound in Oratorio after abuse and trafficking complaints; in January 2025 Interpol arrested a member in Guatemala on trafficking charges. The group had earlier fled child-protection proceedings in Quebec (2013, where authorities sought care for 127 children) and Ontario.
cite: Wikipedia 'Lev Tahor' (citing Reuters, Times of Israel, 2024–2025)

n: ISKCON boarding schools (gurukulas) — acknowledged abuse
who: International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON)
d: In the 1990s ISKCON leaders acknowledged physical, emotional and sexual abuse of children in the movement's boarding schools in the US and India in the 1970s and 1980s, and in 1998 ISKCON itself published an exposé. A $900 million lawsuit filed in Texas in 2002 (the Turley case) led ISKCON temples into Chapter 11 bankruptcy and a $15 million settlement in 2008. ISKCON then set up a Child Protection Office.
cite: Wikipedia 'International Society for Krishna Consciousness' (citing Rochford 2007 and others)

n: Mamou Alliance Academy — missionary children's boarding school, Guinea
who: Christian and Missionary Alliance (C&MA)
d: Mamou Alliance Academy boarded the children of C&MA missionaries in West Africa. After 30 alumni asked for an investigation in 1995, an independent commission of inquiry heard 80 testimonies and reported in April 1998 that the denomination had been negligent; it identified nine offenders, and abuse included sexual molestation and rape. The US C&MA board issued an open letter asking victims' forgiveness.
cover: Alumni wrote to C&MA headquarters about abuse from the 1980s for about ten years before an inquiry was set up.
cite: Independent Commission of Inquiry report, April 1998; Christianity Today, 2010 (via Wikipedia 'Christian and Missionary Alliance')

n: New Tribes Mission — Fanda boarding school, Senegal
who: New Tribes Mission (now Ethnos360)
d: A 2010 report by GRACE (Godly Response to Abuse in the Christian Environment) documented sexual, physical and emotional abuse at the Fanda school that New Tribes Mission ran in Senegal for missionaries' children in the 1980s and 1990s. In 2023 an independent review team (IHART) commissioned by the mission examined historical allegations in Colombia, Indonesia, Mexico, the Philippines, Thailand, the US, Venezuela and Brazil.
cite: GRACE report, 2010; IHART summary report, 2023 (via Wikipedia 'Ethnos360')

n: New Tribes Mission missionary convicted of abusing Katukina girls in Brazil
who: New Tribes Mission
d: Missionary Warren Scott Kennell was arrested at Orlando International Airport in 2013 and admitted molesting four children in Brazil. In July 2014 a US federal court sentenced him to 58 years for abusing Katukina indigenous girls and possessing more than 940 images of child abuse.
cite: WESH-TV 2013; New York Daily News 2014 (via Wikipedia 'Ethnos360')

n: Trokosi — ritual servitude of girls at shrines
who: Traditional shrines (Ewe in Ghana and Togo; Fon in Benin)
d: Under trokosi, shrines take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing; they serve priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty, which defenders deny. Ghana amended its Criminal Code in 1998 to make ritual or customary servitude a crime with a minimum three-year sentence, but the practice continued and no prosecutions are recorded in the source.
cite: Ghana Criminal Code (Amendment) Act 1998 (Act 554); BBC 2001; Africa Recovery 2001 (via Wikipedia 'Trokosi')

n: Devadasi dedication of girls — Karnataka and neighbouring states
who: Temple dedication practice (mostly Dalit girls)
d: Girls, mostly from Dalit families, are dedicated to temple deities and then sexually exploited, despite bans going back to the Bombay Act of 1934, the Andhra Pradesh Act of 1988 and the SC/ST Atrocities Act. A Karnataka government study counted 40,600 devadasis in 2008 and a 2018 university survey found more than 80,000.
cite: Karnataka government study 2008; Karnataka State Women's University 2018; New Indian Express 2020 (via Wikipedia 'Devadasi')
